title: How do you do code / PR reviews (requirement, quality, business logic, exception handling, performance, security, tests, standards)?
shortTitle: How to do code / PR reviews
keyPoints: Start by reading the ticket, then the PR description, then the diff -- confirm the change does exactly what was requested, nothing less and nothing more.
Check business logic by tracing it against realistic cases: money must use BigDecimal, boundaries like zero and negative amounts must be handled.
Exception handling should be specific, transactions should roll back cleanly, and error messages must not leak sensitive data.
Security is non-negotiable: parameterized queries, input validation, authorization checks, no hardcoded secrets.
Tests must cover happy path, failure cases, and boundaries with meaningful assertions; bug fixes need a test that would have caught the bug.
Performance: watch for N+1 queries, unbounded loops, and holding connections or locks too long.
Phrase comments as questions, distinguish blockers from nitpicks, praise good work, and review promptly.

s1_definition.oneliner: A good review verifies requirement, quality, correct business logic, error handling, performance, security, tests, and standards -- catching defects early and spreading knowledge.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Requirement check** -- confirming the change does exactly what the ticket asked, nothing less and nothing more.
- **Quality check** -- meaningful names, small functions, no duplication, readability for future maintainers.
- **Business logic check** -- tracing the logic against realistic cases including boundaries and edge cases.
- **Exception handling** -- specific exceptions, clean rollback, fail-closed behavior, no sensitive data in error messages.
- **Performance check** -- watching for N+1 queries, unbounded data loading, and holding connections too long.
- **Security check** -- parameterized queries, input validation, authorization, no hardcoded secrets.
- **Test check** -- happy path, failure cases, boundaries, and meaningful assertions.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of a code review as the supervisor sign-off before a large transaction is posted at National Bank of India. Before money moves, a second officer checks that the form matches what the customer asked (requirement), is filled in neatly (quality), that the math is right (business logic), that it handles a frozen or overdrawn account (exception handling), that it will not jam the queue at month-end (performance), that nobody can tamper with it (security), that there is a receipt (tests), and that it follows standard procedure (standards).

sections.s6_takeaway:
A thorough code review works through a consistent set of dimensions. Start with the requirement to confirm the change matches the ticket. Check quality and maintainability -- meaningful names, small functions, no duplication. Trace the business logic against realistic cases, especially boundary conditions, and confirm money uses BigDecimal. Check that exceptions are specific, transactions roll back cleanly, and error messages do not leak sensitive data.

Performance and security are never optional in banking. Watch for N+1 queries, unbounded data loading, and holding connections too long. Check for parameterized queries, proper authorization, and no hardcoded secrets. Confirm tests cover the happy path, failure cases, and boundaries with meaningful assertions.

The human side matters as much as the technical. Phrase comments as questions, separate blockers from nitpicks, praise good work, and review promptly so you never block the team. A healthy review culture is one of the strongest quality tools a team has.

Remember one sentence: a good review checks requirement, logic, security, and tests in that order, phrasing every comment as a helpful question rather than a criticism.
